content.intro: In this lesson, you will study understanding scanner input behavior with a short explanation, an original visual map, a Java example, and a check you can perform yourself. Focus on the relationship between the rule and the behavior rather than memorizing isolated syntax.
content.why_it_matters: This concept matters because it helps you turn raw console input into validated data and provide clear feedback for invalid values. In this lesson, focus on token-based reading and use a minimal example to check what the rule actually guarantees.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Console input is external data. Distinguish token-reading from line-reading, validate parsed values and ranges, and make malformed or missing input produce a clear response. Apply that reasoning specifically to token-based reading and confirm the result with the example or a targeted test. The important habit is to make the assumptions explicit and use the code example as a small experiment.

content_blocks.title: How the pieces fit
content_blocks.text: Connect token-based reading with line-based reading before choosing an implementation. The example is a small, observable case; extend it by changing one input and checking a boundary, invalid value, or compatibility limit where relevant.

items.text: A method gives a named contract to a unit of behavior. Keep responsibilities focused, define clear parameter and return types, and test typical, boundary, and invalid cases independently.

items.title: Handling malformed input
items.text: Treat console input as untrusted text. Validate format and range before using it, account for token-versus-line reading, and give users a clear way to correct invalid input.
